profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting for a proposed client-facing feature called "Risk Network Explorer" inside an enterprise risk intelligence platform. The feature is based on a weighted risk network built from public financial disclosures and is intended to help corporate risk teams classify risks, spot specialization gaps in risk identification across business units or peer firms, and distinguish independently severe risks from emerging systemic ones. The agenda is to review the existing proposal deck and prototype screens, judge whether the design faithfully represents the underlying methodology, identify any gaps before the steering committee review, and decide whether the proposal is ready to move into a pilot. The expected outcome is provisional approval of the design direction, plus a short list of revisions before the steering committee presentation.

members.name: Priya Nair
members.expertise: Risk modeling, network analysis, regulatory risk frameworks, methodological validation
members.background: Priya leads the internal research team that adapted weighted risk-network methods from financial disclosure data into a commercial analytics concept and has previously worked in bank stress-testing and model governance.
members.private_state: She wants the design to preserve the methodological meaning of the research so the pilot is not oversold, and she is especially concerned that product packaging will flatten important caveats about clustering, stability, and emergent risk interpretation.
hidden_assumptions: If the team says the product uses a "classification framework," that means the network-derived modules themselves become the primary risk classes presented in the analysis.
A design is only "pilot-ready" if the methodology is defensible under review, including stability notes, caveats, and the latest validated network run.
When people refer to the "current network," they mean the most recent post-adjustment analytical run from Friday, even if some design assets have not been refreshed.
A firm's "coverage" of risk identification means whether it touches a module at all, because the specialization finding is about breadth across classes rather than intensity within one class.

members.name: Evan Brooks
members.role: Senior Product Manager, Risk Intelligence Platform
members.expertise: B2B analytics products, client-facing dashboard design, pilot commercialization, stakeholder communication
members.background: Evan owns the roadmap for new risk analytics modules and has spent the last six years translating technical models into executive dashboards for insurers, banks, and corporate risk teams.
members.private_state: He wants the review to end with approval to take the concept to the steering committee and then into a limited client pilot, and he is trying to keep the story intuitive and visually consistent with the rest of the platform.
hidden_assumptions: If the team says "classification framework," that means a way to organize insights behind the scenes while still presenting results through the client's existing risk taxonomy in the UI.
A design is "pilot-ready" once the narrative is commercially coherent, the screens are clickable, and caveats are contained well enough for a committee audience.

When people mention the "current network," they mean the version already frozen into the latest review deck and prototype, because design review is about the present artifact, not the most recent analytical rerun.
A "coverage" view should show intensity or share by module so users can rank where attention is concentrated, not just whether a module appears at least once.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to use the network modules as the "classification framework."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes the discovered network modules are the actual risk classes that should structure the analysis and be shown as the primary organizing scheme.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes the modules are an analytic layer that should be translated into or nested within the client's existing taxonomy rather than replacing it in the interface.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase "classification framework" sounds fully aligned and both positions are compatible at a high level, so neither person feels a need to unpack whether the framework is user-visible or mostly interpretive.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the proposal should be "pilot-ready" after this review.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the design can proceed only once the methodology is documented with validation notes, caveats about bias and stability, and the latest vetted analytical outputs.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the design can proceed once the committee can understand the story, the prototype looks coherent, and any caveats are packaged unobtrusively enough not to block a pilot conversation.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In design reviews, "pilot-ready" is a normal shorthand for progress, and both participants are used to the term without explicitly listing the acceptance threshold they each have in mind.

misalignment_points.topic: Which version is the current network
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to "the current network" and assume they are discussing the same graph and module structure.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the Friday analytical rerun that changed weights after outlier treatment and slightly shifted the modular structure.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the Wednesday deck and prototype assets, which still show the earlier graph that marketing already formatted for review.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both versions are recent, both are internally called the latest version in their own workflows, and the design meeting focuses on high-level interpretation rather than line-by-line asset provenance.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the design should show "coverage" to demonstrate specialization in risk identification.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 expects coverage to be computed as firm-by-module presence, where a firm is counted as covering a class if it identifies any risk in that module.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects coverage to be shown as the share or intensity of mentions by module so users can compare concentration and dominant areas.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They both think a coverage view obviously communicates specialization, and the methodological choice hides inside the chart logic rather than appearing as a headline design decision.

turns.inner_thought: I need to make sure this hasn't drifted into a glossy product story that strips out the methodological meaning. If we're saying it's pilot-ready after this review, that has to mean the approach is defensible: validation appendix included, caveats on clustering and stability explicit, and the latest vetted outputs carried through. Otherwise we're taking something forward that I wouldn't want in front of model governance or a skeptical client risk team.
turns.utterance: Thanks, everyone. Before we get into the screens, I just want to confirm that the design still reflects the research faithfully and that we're aiming to come out of today with something that's pilot-ready.

turns.inner_thought: The goal is to get sign-off on a coherent concept we can take to steering. I need Priya comfortable enough with the story, but the interface should stay consistent with the existing platform. In my mind the classification framework is the analytic spine behind the experience, not a replacement for the client's taxonomy. The current network is what's already in the deck and prototype, and the coverage view should show where signal is concentrated so executives can read it in seconds.
turns.utterance: Absolutely. The prototype is organized around the classification framework, a coverage view, an emerging-risk panel, and the supporting visuals from the current network. The idea is that the story hangs together cleanly from classification to specialization to systemic signal.

turns.inner_thought: Good, as long as the modules themselves are what clients see as the risk classes. That's the substance of the work; otherwise we're just decorating an old taxonomy with network language. And when we say current network, I mean the Friday rerun after outlier treatment, because the module structure shifted enough to matter analytically.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. For me, the key is that the modules come through clearly as the classification framework, because the modular structure in the current network is really the core analytical contribution here.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, exactly—the modules should be present and legible, but within the taxonomy tabs users already know. I do not want to re-platform navigation for a pilot or ask clients to learn a whole new information architecture. If we keep the framework intuitive, the committee will see it as adoptable rather than disruptive.
turns.utterance: Agreed. My thought is that users encounter those modules through a classification framework that feels intuitive in the flow, so they can orient quickly without the experience becoming unfamiliar.

turns.inner_thought: Now the specialization point. The important finding is breadth across classes: some firms touch many modules, some only a few. Coverage should demonstrate whether a firm identifies anything in a module at all. If we blur that into volume, we lose the point about narrow versus broad identification patterns.
turns.utterance: On the specialization slide, I do think the coverage view is doing useful work. It helps show that some firms are focused on only a subset of the available classes, which is an important part of the story.

turns.inner_thought: A heatmap would make this much more legible. If coverage shows share by module, users can instantly see where each firm's risk attention is concentrated and compare peers. That's the kind of visual steering committee members respond to; binary presence is too flat for a dashboard.
turns.utterance: I agree, and I think we can make that even clearer. I’d like to turn the coverage view into a heatmap so the pattern stands out immediately and users can see where each firm is concentrated at a glance.

turns.inner_thought: The emerging-risk panel is directionally fine, but I need guardrails if this is going forward. Pilot-ready means the package includes the validation appendix, notes on bias and stability limitations, and enough methodological framing that no one mistakes emergent centrality for a simplistic severity score.
turns.utterance: The emerging-risk panel works for me in principle. I’d just want the pilot-ready package to include the validation appendix and a note on bias and stability limits so the framing stays disciplined.

turns.inner_thought: I can accommodate caveats, but they cannot dominate the committee conversation. For pilot-ready, what I need is a crisp narrative, a clickable prototype, and caveats packaged in a way that reassures without bogging us down. If this turns into a methodology defense, we won't get approval to test with clients.
turns.utterance: That’s fair. From my side, pilot-ready means we have a clean storyline, a clickable flow for the committee, and caveats that are there but don’t overwhelm the demo.

turns.inner_thought: One concrete fix before anything goes upstairs: the systemic-impact chart needs to reflect the Friday rerun. After the weighting adjustment, the module boundaries moved slightly, and if the visuals still reflect the earlier structure, the interpretation of which risks are bridging versus contained could be off.
turns.utterance: One specific ask from me: can we refresh the systemic-impact chart so it matches the current network after the weighting adjustment? The module boundaries moved slightly, and I want the visual to stay aligned.

turns.inner_thought: I’ll polish the assets we already have in the prototype and keep momentum. The current network in the deck is what the committee will see, and I don't want to reopen formatted visuals unless absolutely necessary. I'll interpret her note as a light clean-up, not a rerender from a newer analytical run. If I can bring a refined, pilot-ready package, we should get approval to proceed.
turns.utterance: Yes, understood. I’ll polish the deck using the current network already in the prototype, tighten the flow, and bring the revised pilot-ready package to the steering committee.
